# Quantum channels and open-system dynamics {#sec-open-systems}

## From inaccessible degrees of freedom to a map

A system need not be thermally equilibrated to be mixed. An unobserved photon can carry away phase information; a random unitary can produce classical uncertainty; a measurement can leave a record that is discarded. The common description is a quantum channel, a map taking input density matrices to output density matrices.

Assume initially that system and environment are uncorrelated, $\rho\otimes\ket0\bra0_E$. Let a joint unitary $V$ act, and discard $E$:

$$
\mathcal E(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\left[V(\rho\otimes\ket0\bra0_E)V^\dagger\right].
$$ {#eq-channel-dilation}

The initial-product assumption matters. If the input is correlated with $E$, a single channel on arbitrary system states need not describe the reduced dynamics. The environment can always be enlarged to purify its initially mixed state.

Choose an orthonormal basis $\ket a_E$ and define $K_a={}_E\bra a V\ket0_E$. Inserting this basis into the partial trace gives

$$
\mathcal E(\rho)=\sum_aK_a\rho K_a^\dagger,\qquad
\sum_aK_a^\dagger K_a=I.
$$ {#eq-kraus}

The second identity follows from $V^\dagger V=I$ and guarantees trace preservation. Each term is positive on positive inputs. The same construction remains positive when an arbitrary spectator system is included. This is complete positivity. A completely positive trace-preserving map is abbreviated CPTP.

Ordinary positivity is insufficient because the input system may be entangled with a spectator. Matrix transposition preserves positivity on a single system but is not completely positive. Applied to one half of a Bell pair, it produces a matrix with a negative eigenvalue. It cannot be a deterministic physical channel.

Kraus operators are not unique. Replacing $K_a$ by $\widetilde K_b=\sum_a w_{ba}K_a$ with an isometry $w$ gives the same channel. Thus a particular list of Kraus outcomes is additional structure until a physical measurement of the environment selects that list.

## Measurement, selection, and discarded records

A measurement instrument consists of completely positive maps $\mathcal E_a$ with $\sum_a\mathcal E_a$ trace preserving. Outcome $a$ has probability $p_a=\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal E_a(\rho)$, and the conditioned state is $\rho_a=\mathcal E_a(\rho)/p_a$. The map $\rho\mapsto\rho_a$ is nonlinear because of this normalization. The unconditioned state is the linear average $\sum_ap_a\rho_a$.

For a projective $Z$ measurement on a qubit,

$$
\mathcal M_Z(\rho)=P_0\rho P_0+P_1\rho P_1
=\frac12(\rho+Z\rho Z).
$$

If the input is $\ket+$, either conditioned state is pure, while the discarded-record output is $I/2$. A monitored trajectory and its record-averaged density matrix are different physical objects. They may undergo different phase transitions.

To keep the record explicitly, introduce a classical register:

$$
\rho_{SC}=\sum_ap_a\rho_a\otimes\ket a\bra a_C.
$$

Tracing $C$ produces the unconditioned state. Reading $C$ can reveal correlations absent from the density matrix of $S$ alone. Later comparisons with charge sharpening, spin-glass-like trajectory order, and decoding will always specify which records are available.

## Three elementary channels

### Dephasing

With probability $p$ apply $Z$:

$$
\mathcal D_p(\rho)=(1-p)\rho+pZ\rho Z.
$$ {#eq-qubit-dephasing}

In the $Z$ basis, diagonal entries remain fixed and off-diagonal entries are multiplied by $1-2p$. The Bloch vector transforms as $(r_x,r_y,r_z)\mapsto((1-2p)r_x,(1-2p)r_y,r_z)$. At $p=1/2$ all coherence in this basis disappears. At $p=1$ the map is a reversible unitary, so a noise parameter need not be globally monotone unless its domain is specified. We usually take $0\leq p\leq1/2$.

Composition gives

$$
\mathcal D_p\mathcal D_q=\mathcal D_{p+q-2pq}.
$$

The attenuation factors multiply. This simple identity lets us translate finite-time dephasing into a noise probability.

### Amplitude damping

Spontaneous relaxation from $\ket1$ to $\ket0$ is described by

$$
K_0=\ket0\bra0+\sqrt{1-\gamma}\ket1\bra1,
\qquad K_1=\sqrt\gamma\ket0\bra1.
$$

Then $\rho_{11}\mapsto(1-\gamma)\rho_{11}$ and $\rho_{01}\mapsto\sqrt{1-\gamma}\rho_{01}$. The maximally mixed state does not remain maximally mixed. A channel satisfying $\mathcal E(I)=I$ is called unital; amplitude damping is not unital. Unitality and trace preservation are different conditions.

### Erasure and replacement

The map $\mathcal R(\rho)=\tau\operatorname{Tr}\rho$ replaces every input by a fixed state $\tau$. It is CPTP and destroys all input information. If arbitrary one-way local channels defined phase equivalence, every state could be sent to a trivial product state. Any useful mixed-state phase definition therefore needs additional conditions, such as a reverse channel, local reversibility, or symmetry constraints.

## The Choi representation

Let $d=\dim\mathcal H$ and $\ket\Phi=d^{-1/2}\sum_i\ket i\ket i$. Define

$$
J_{\mathcal E}=(\mathcal E\otimes\mathrm{id})(\ket\Phi\bra\Phi).
$$

Complete positivity is equivalent to $J_{\mathcal E}\geq0$, and trace preservation is equivalent to $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{out}}J_{\mathcal E}=I_{\mathrm{in}}/d$. Conversely,

$$
\mathcal E(A)=d\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{in}}
\left[J_{\mathcal E}(I\otimes A^T)\right].
$$

This follows by expanding $\ket\Phi\bra\Phi=d^{-1}\sum_{ij}\ket i\bra j\otimes\ket i\bra j$. It provides a finite matrix test for physicality and makes clear that a channel has more structure than its action on one selected state.

The Choi matrix of a channel should not be confused with vectorizing a density matrix as $\ket\rho\!\rangle$. Both use doubled spaces, but one represents a map and the other a state. The canonical vector $\ket{\sqrt\rho}\!\rangle$ is a third construction, with yet another normalization.

## Continuous time and the Lindblad equation

Markovian time-homogeneous dynamics assumes $\mathcal E_{t+s}=\mathcal E_t\mathcal E_s$ and $\mathcal E_0=\mathrm{id}$. Under the usual continuity assumptions in finite dimension, $\mathcal E_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ with a generator of the Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad form [@gks1976; @lindblad1976]:

$$
\partial_t\rho=\mathcal L(\rho)
=-i[H,\rho]+\sum_a\left(L_a\rho L_a^\dagger
-\frac12\{L_a^\dagger L_a,\rho\}\right).
$$ {#eq-lindblad-foundation}

The $L_a$ are jump operators; rates may be absorbed into their normalization. The anticommutator terms compensate the probability lost from no-jump evolution.

To see the structure, take a small step $dt$ with

$$
K_0=I-dt\left(iH+\frac12\sum_aL_a^\dagger L_a\right),
\qquad K_a=\sqrt{dt}\,L_a.
$$

Then $\sum_\alpha K_\alpha^\dagger K_\alpha=I+O(dt^2)$. Expanding the Kraus sum to first order gives @eq-lindblad-foundation. The exact exponential is CPTP. A first-order Euler step is only an approximation and need not stay positive for a large step.

Trace preservation follows directly by cyclicity. Hermiticity is also preserved. The nontrivial positivity guarantee comes from the generator's structure, not from these two easier checks.

### Worked example: continuous dephasing

For $L=\sqrt\kappa Z$, the master equation is $\dot\rho=\kappa(Z\rho Z-\rho)$. The off-diagonal equation is $\dot\rho_{01}=-2\kappa\rho_{01}$, so

$$
\rho_{01}(t)=e^{-2\kappa t}\rho_{01}(0),\qquad
p(t)=\frac{1-e^{-2\kappa t}}2.
$$

The diagonal entries remain fixed. Complete dephasing is reached only at infinite time. A collective or many-body transition may nevertheless occur at a finite $p_c<1/2$, hence at a finite time. Conversely, in some one-dimensional models only the infinite-time limit has long-range nonlinear order.

## Heisenberg evolution and conservation laws

The adjoint generator is defined by $\operatorname{Tr}[O\mathcal L(\rho)]=\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal L^\dagger(O)\rho]$. It is

$$
\mathcal L^\dagger(O)=i[H,O]+\sum_a
\left(L_a^\dagger OL_a-\frac12\{L_a^\dagger L_a,O\}\right).
$$

An observable $Q$ is conserved in mean for all states if $\mathcal L^\dagger(Q)=0$. The sufficient conditions $[H,Q]=[L_a,Q]=0$ are stronger: each jump preserves every charge sector. That is the dynamical strong-symmetry condition relevant to this book. Covariance under conjugation by a symmetry is weaker and can allow jumps that exchange charge with the environment.

For example, local raising and lowering jumps can preserve covariance under $e^{i\theta Q}$ because their phases cancel between $L_a$ and $L_a^\dagger$, yet they do not preserve fixed-$Q$ sectors. These distinctions are developed precisely in @sec-symmetry.

## Stationary states, gaps, and mixing

A stationary state satisfies $\mathcal L(\rho_*)=0$. A stationary manifold may contain multiple states, especially if sectors cannot communicate. Uniqueness must be stated either globally or within a selected sector.

The spectrum of $\mathcal L$ lies in the closed left half-plane for a finite CPTP semigroup. A positive spectral gap is the smallest nonzero decay rate $-\operatorname{Re}\lambda$ after stationary and other nondecaying modes are treated appropriately. It is tempting to equate its inverse with equilibration time. That can fail.

Define a trace-distance mixing time within an invariant sector by

$$
t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\epsilon)=\inf\left\{t:
\sup_{\rho\ \mathrm{in\ sector}}\frac12\|e^{t\mathcal L}(\rho)-\rho_*\|_1\leq\epsilon\right\}.
$$

Even when eigenvalues are known, coefficients, nonorthogonal eigenvectors, Jordan blocks, and the size of the state space can introduce size-dependent factors. A uniform spectral gap alone does not establish size-independent mixing. This is relevant to proposed links between steady-state SW-SSB and rapid mixing.

## Local channels and causal structure

A finite-depth local channel circuit has a bounded number of layers; each layer contains disjoint gates supported on bounded regions. Information can propagate only a bounded distance through a fixed-depth circuit. A local Lindbladian with bounded, short-range terms has an approximate causal cone, with exponentially small tails outside a Lieb-Robinson-type cone. Finite-time dynamics is therefore related to shallow channels, but the desired accuracy may introduce logarithmic corrections in system size.

Depth, range, norm bounds, and error convention must all be specified before claiming that a phase cannot be transformed locally. A circuit of depth proportional to $L$ can communicate across the sample and is outside fixed-depth stability statements.

The environment also matters. A collection of fresh, initially uncorrelated local ancillas is different from preloading a globally correlated environment with the state one wants to prepare. Allowing the latter would insert the order by assumption.

## Exercises and worked solutions

### 1. Complete positivity of transposition

Apply transposition to the second qubit of $\ket{\Phi^+}\bra{\Phi^+}$ and find the spectrum.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The partially transposed matrix is half the swap operator: $\frac12\sum_{ij}\ket i\bra j\otimes\ket j\bra i$. Swap has eigenvalue $+1$ on the three-dimensional symmetric subspace and $-1$ on the singlet. The spectrum is $1/2,1/2,1/2,-1/2$. Hence transposition cannot act as a deterministic channel on an arbitrary subsystem entangled with a spectator.
:::

### 2. An environment realization of dephasing

Construct an isometry producing @eq-qubit-dephasing, and identify the record basis.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Take $W\ket\psi=\sqrt{1-p}\ket\psi\ket0_E+\sqrt p\,Z\ket\psi\ket1_E$. Orthogonality of the environment states gives $W^\dagger W=I$. Tracing $E$ yields the Kraus sum. Measuring $E$ in this basis reveals which random unitary occurred. Measuring a different basis gives a different unraveling of the same reduced channel.
:::

### 3. Strong symmetry of pair noise

Let $U=\prod_iX_i$ and let each bond jump be $L_{ij}=\sqrt\kappa Z_iZ_j$. Show that the sector of $U$ is conserved. Compare a single-site $Z_i$ jump.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Conjugating $Z_iZ_j$ by $U$ produces two minus signs and leaves it unchanged. Thus every pair jump commutes with $U$, preserving each eigenspace in every trajectory. A single $Z_i$ anticommutes with $U$ and flips its eigenvalue. The single-site dissipator is still covariant under $U$ because the two signs in $Z_i\rho Z_i$ cancel. It preserves weak symmetry of the averaged state but exchanges strong-charge sectors.
:::

### 4. What does a gap prove?

Suppose a bound has the form $\|\rho(t)-\rho_*\|_1\leq C_Ne^{-\Delta t}$, with $C_N=e^{aN}$. Estimate the time needed to reach error $\epsilon$ when $\Delta$ is independent of $N$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
It is sufficient to take $t\geq(aN+\ln(1/\epsilon))/\Delta$. Thus this estimate allows a mixing time linear in $N$ despite a constant gap. Better estimates may exist, but the eigenvalue statement alone does not supply them. One must control the prefactor or an appropriate stronger mixing inequality.
:::

### 5. Selection versus averaging

Starting from a two-spin cat, projectively measure $Z_1$. Give the conditioned and unconditioned states and identify which have a definite value of $X_1X_2$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The outcomes give $\ket{00}$ or $\ket{11}$ with equal probability. Discarding the outcome gives their classical coin. The input cat is an eigenvector of $X_1X_2$ with eigenvalue $+1$. Neither selected branch nor the unconditioned coin is supported in that eigenspace. The coin remains invariant under conjugation by $X_1X_2$, whereas the selected branches do not. This is an explicit channel-induced loss of strong symmetry, distinct from spontaneous breaking diagnosed in a strongly symmetric state.
:::
